- _Evidence:_ D3; R:ba-authz.

**ADR-25. Exclusive binding: one live Nest app per better-auth instance. A binding whose app never finished bootstrapping can be taken over.**

- _From:_ [B] B-ADR-06, [C] C-ADR-15.
- _Rejected:_
  - [A]'s attach/detach per app with ALS-based host routing. It is complex, ambiguous for calls outside any scope (A falls back to "most recently attached"), and it silently allows double side effects;
  - v1's unconditional exclusivity: a module whose `onModuleInit` threw after the core module had bound left the instance bound for good, so every following test failed with `INSTANCE_ALREADY_BOUND` and hid the original error;
  - registering `app.close()` with `afterEach` only (the reviewer's first option): it needs a runner hook in scope, which a runner-agnostic helper cannot assume, and it does not help a failed `init()`.
- _Rationale:_ a forgotten `app.close()` or a double import becomes a loud boot error, and hooks never leak across apps.
- _Revised in v2_ `[R1:SEC-r1-15]`: the binding records `bootstrapped` (set in `onApplicationBootstrap`). `bind()` throws only against a bootstrapped owner and takes over any other with `W_INSTANCE_TAKEN_OVER`. `initTestApp` closes the previous test app bound to the same instance (ADR-51).
- _Revised in v3_ `[R2:NEST-r2-05]`: a second `bind()` from the same application is a no-op, and the core module's lifecycle work runs once per application, because `NestMicroservice.init()` runs `onModuleInit` and `onApplicationBootstrap` twice and v2 answered its own app with `INSTANCE_ALREADY_BOUND` (ADR-62).
- _Evidence:_ R:ref-impl §5.3.

**ADR-26. Named better-auth instances are supported in 1.0; dynamically swappable instances are not.**

- _From:_ [A] §5.5, [C] §5.5.
- _Rejected:_
  - [B] B-ADR-18, one instance in the first release with a seam kept: reference issues #51/#79 show real demand, and the token and metadata design already supports it at low cost;
  - dynamic instances: they conflict with better-auth's construction-time model.
- _Revised in v2_ `[R1:SEC-r1-11, NEST-r1-09]`: two instances in one app interact in ways v1 did not check. They must not share cookie names on overlapping scopes (ADR-47), and only the default instance declares platforms and transports (ADR-45).
- _Evidence:_ R:ref-issues #51, #79.

**ADR-27. Built-in policies live in per-plugin subpaths (`./admin`, `./organization`, `./api-key`), and `freshSession` lives in the session unit. There are no role-name decorators in 1.0.**

- _From:_ subpaths are [A]; no roles is [B][C].
- _Rejected:_
  - [B]/[C] admin and org policies in the root entry: that blurs "one unit per better-auth plugin";
  - [A] an opt-in exact-mirror `RolePolicy` in `./admin`: it would reimplement admin internals such as `adminUserIds` and `defaultRole` (§17 Q1).
- _Rationale:_ this mirrors better-auth's own plugin-first layout.
- _Revised in v2_ `[R1:NEST-r1-07]`: v1 said "`freshSession` in core". It names the `'session'` kind, so it belongs to the session unit (`src/extensions/session`), which the root entry re-exports like `httpTransport()` (ADR-41).
- _Revised in v3_ `[R2:BA-r2-08, SEC-r2-06]`: organization refs always resolve to a validated organization ID, the default one included, and no slug ref ships (ADR-63).

**ADR-28. Authoritative identity reads are a plan attribute: one `getSession` with `disableCookieCache` when stateful. The route, the instance or a requirement can ask for it. `freshSession()` is 0-I/O.**

- _From:_ [C] (freshness in the plan); [A] (0-I/O fresh-session policy).
- _Rejected:_
  - [A]'s separate `AuthoritativeSessionPolicy`: a second read per request;
  - [B]'s `FreshSessionPolicy` re-reading the session: unnecessary, because `createdAt` is immutable.
- _Revised in v2_ `[R1:SEC-r1-04]`: besides `@RequireAuth({ authoritative: true })` and `session.freshness`, a requirement or its policy can raise the route's freshness with `freshIdentity`. The admin policy does so by default (ADR-36). Because freshness is part of the principal memo key, it is still one read.
- _Revised in v3_ `[R2:BA-r2-06]`: an authoritative read also requires that the get-session endpoint produced the session, never a before-hook (ADR-54). v2's authoritative read accepted an API key's mocked session under `enableSessionForAPIKeys`, which better-auth's own authoritative read never does.
- _Evidence:_ LEAD-V3; `BA/api/routes/session.ts:520-539`.

**ADR-29. `@CurrentSession()`/`@CurrentUser()` imply a session principal (a route that admits another kind fails boot, B15 `PRINCIPAL_PARAM_CONFLICT`), and `@Public()` combined with them fails boot (B15).**

- _From:_ [C] C-ADR-22 and draft C's boot check 12 (this document's B15).
- _Rejected:_ [A]/[B] returning `null` there, which lies against an `AuthSession` annotation and hides the migration trap left by the old `@AllowAnonymous`.
- _Revised in v2_ `[R1:NEST-r1-10, NEST-r1-07]`: renamed from `@Session()` (ADR-24). The rule is no longer a branch on `'session'` in the guard: the decorators are built with `definePrincipalParam`, which records `{ kind, reason }` as plan data, and the guard compares data (ADR-41). A third-party kind can therefore have its own constrained decorator.
- _Revised in v3_ `[R2:NEST-r2-08]`: the guard no longer compares a principal's kind with the handler's param decorators at runtime. Every plan comes from the planner, which checks the constraint at boot (B15), including kinds that `defaultRequirements` name; v2 kept the runtime comparison only for plans a `planFor` override produced, and that seam is gone (ADR-58).

**ADR-30. Param decorators are synchronous and read the scope, then the invocation and carrier stamps; otherwise they throw.**

- _From:_ [A] (carrier stamp, throw); [C] (sync, throw); [L] (scope first).
- _Rejected:_ [B] B-ADR-10, a sync factory plus a DI pipe that resolves lazily even without a guard. It hides unguarded routes, does I/O in the pipe stage, and interacts with global `ValidationPipe` configuration.
- _Revised in v2_ `[R1:NEST-r1-01, NEST-r1-08]`: there are two stamps now. The principal stays on the per-request carrier; values a policy published (`@ActiveOrganizationId()`) are stamped on the **invocation** object, so a GraphQL field never reads a sibling field's organization (ADR-37). Because the decorators throw when nothing was stamped, a guard replaced in a test needs `stampPrincipal()` (ADR-51), which writes a third kind, the test stamp, verified by args-element identity and copied into the scope by the interceptors (§7.8 item 3). The throw itself is generic as thrown (`atRequest`, ADR-43), because it fires where no transport maps errors.
- _Revised in v3_ `[R2:NEST-r2-06, NEST-r2-14]`: the principal stamps changed. The guard stamps each invocation object with that invocation's own result, and the operation-wide carrier with a map by memo key (freshness and source set); a reader without its own guard run (an inheriting field resolver) takes a carrier entry only when the instance has exactly one, else it throws `NO_AUTH_RESULT`. v2's one-entry-per-instance carrier was last-writer-wins, so a field resolver could read a principal of a kind its root field never admitted. The decorators read the handler plan's instance and take no `instance` option.
- _Evidence:_ LEAD-V7; LEAD-V34; LEAD-EXP-7; R:nest-di §4.3; EXP-B:E6 (the pipe approach works, but was not chosen).

**ADR-31. Plugin handles are unbound in `onApplicationShutdown`.**

- _From:_ [C].
- _Rejected:_ `onModuleDestroy` ([A][B]): it runs before the HTTP server stops accepting requests, so in-flight requests would lose their hooks.
- _Evidence:_ Nest 11.1.17 `core/nest-application-context.js:126-133`.

**ADR-32. HEAD and OPTIONS are passed through to better-auth.**

- _From:_ [B] B-Q10, [C] C-ADR-21.
- _Rejected:_ answering HEAD as a body-less GET. It would run GET side effects (session refresh writes) under a different method, and better-auth deliberately answers HEAD itself (404).
- _Evidence:_ R:ba-core §3.1.

**ADR-33. CORS belongs to the host. The library guarantees host CORS reaches auth routes and ships `betterAuthCorsOrigin(auth)`: better-auth's post-init trusted origins, exact origins only by default, and a throw for function-valued `trustedOrigins`.**

- _From:_ [A] A-ADR-7, [B] B-ADR-14, [C] C-ADR-05. The throw is [C].
- _Rejected:_
  - library-owned CORS derived from `trustedOrigins` (the reference, @nestm): exact-match bugs with wildcards (#69), Fastify double registration (#52), app-wide side effects (#95), different behavior per platform;
  - [A]/[B]'s helper silently using init-time values of a request-dependent function;
  - v1's helper, which delegated to `$context.isTrustedOrigin` as is. It missed origins that plugins add in `init()`, and it honored wildcards, so `https://*.vercel.app`, trusted for CSRF and redirects, gained credentialed read access to every Nest route once the helper was used app-wide;
  - the reviewer's "exact **https** origins only": it would reject `http://localhost:3000`, which every development setup uses. Exact `http(s)` origins are allowed; wildcards and custom schemes need `allowPatterns: true`.
- _Revised in v2_ `[R1:BA-r1-11, SEC-r1-17]`: the helper reads the shared `TrustedOrigins` resolver (the same set the origin check uses, ADR-34) and defaults to exact origins. The docs recommend an explicit allow-list for app routes and show how to scope the helper to the auth mount.
- _Evidence:_ R:ba-integrations §0.2; R:ref-issues §3.4; EXP-B:E1/E4; EXP-C4/C6; LEAD-V17; test `LIB-cors-helper` (init-contributed origin with preflight ACAO, patterns only with `allowPatterns`, the mount-only scope, the throw for function-valued `trustedOrigins`).

**ADR-34. The kernel applies better-auth's origin rule to every unsafe operation whose browser leg carries a cookie, whatever credential authenticated it: unsafe HTTP methods, GraphQL mutations over HTTP, and every WebSocket message and every GraphQL operation a WebSocket carries; and better-auth's form-CSRF rule to handlers that forward auth cookies. It is on by default and strict about a missing origin.**

- _Forced by:_ `[R1:SEC-r1-01]` (blocker), `[R1:BA-r1-03]`. v1 listed "origin/CSRF" as something `auth.handler` does. It does, but only for its own routes: `validateOrigin` is router middleware and returns early without `ctx.request` (LEAD-V16). In REV-SEC:`probe-bridge-foreign.mjs` the guard's `getSession` accepted an evil-origin cookie request that the router rejected with 403. With `sameSite: 'none'` cookies, which better-auth documents for cross-domain setups, or an attacker on a sibling subdomain, that meant cross-site form posts to Nest routes, cross-site mutations and Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking.
- _Decision:_ one kernel step (`OriginCheck`, §7.10), fed by data every transport supplies (`TransportCall.browser`). It reuses better-auth's trusted-origin set (post-init, ADR-33), its matcher (`$context.isTrustedOrigin`), its skip flags and its error codes. A request without a cookie on its browser leg is never checked in the default mode, whatever other credentials it carries, and RPC has no browser leg. Opt-outs: `@SkipOriginCheck()` per route, `originCheck.mode: 'off'` per instance (B19 warns in production).
- _Rejected:_
  - host responsibility (v1; BA's option 1): the library creates these cookie-carrying surfaces and knows which operations are unsafe and where their browser leg is; the host knows neither. CORS does not apply to form posts or WebSocket upgrades at all;
  - opt-in only, a `@RequireSameOrigin()` requirement or a module flag that is off by default (BA's option 3): secure by default (better-auth principle P8, §0.2) means the unsafe configuration is the one you have to ask for;
  - a per-transport option (`originCheck: 'cookie' | 'always' | 'off'` on the WS and GraphQL transports, BA's suggested fix): the rule would be implemented once per transport, third-party transports would have to reimplement it, and HTTP app routes would still be uncovered. Transports supply facts; the kernel owns the rule;
  - our own origin matcher or allow-list: a second, drifting definition of "trusted" (R1). We call `isTrustedOrigin` with the merged set;
  - SEC's proposed default for a missing origin, "allow when no browser signal is present at all". better-auth's own routes answer 403 `MISSING_OR_NULL_ORIGIN` in that case, so the strict default is the faithful one. The exemption also misses the client it was meant for: Node's `fetch`, which SSR servers use, sends `sec-fetch-mode: cors` with no `Origin` (LEAD-EXP-4). The lenient rule ships as `originCheck.missingOrigin: 'allow-non-browser'`, keyed on `Origin`, `Referer` and `Sec-Fetch-Site` only (§17 Q15);
  - relying on `SameSite` cookies: better-auth's cross-domain guidance turns it off, and it never separates sibling subdomains.
- _Rationale:_ it extends better-auth's secure-by-default cookie model to exactly the surfaces this library adds, with better-auth's own notion of trust, and leaves callers without cookies (bearer, API-key and RPC clients) alone. The cost is a trusted `Origin` header on cookie-bearing unsafe requests from non-browser clients and from cross-origin clients that also send a token, which better-auth already demands on its own routes (§17 Q14, Q26, RK21).
- _Known limit:_ better-auth exposes no function for this rule, so the kernel **mirrors** it. The mirror was written against 1.7.4; the `Origin: null` + `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin` inference reached better-auth's router only in 1.7.2, so on 1.7.0 and 1.7.1 the kernel is more lenient than the router for that one same-origin case (LEAD-V33). `LIB-origin-differential`, run against the router on every better-auth version in the matrix, detects further drift (§14.5, RK20).
- _Revised in v3_ `[R2:SEC-r2-01, NEST-r2-13, SEC-r2-03, SEC-r2-05, SEC-r2-08]`:
  - **The explicit-credential exemption is gone.** v2 skipped the check when a `Bearer`/`DPoP` authorization or a source's credential header was present, without asking whether it authenticated. On socket.io and graphql-ws those headers come from `handshake.auth` and `connectionParams`, which the attacking page chooses, so a junk token switched the check off while the victim's cookie authenticated (REV2-SEC:`probe-origin-bearer-exempt.mjs`). ADR-34's claim that the library "knows which credential authenticated the call" was wrong: it only saw which headers were present. The kernel now validates whenever the browser leg's own headers carry a cookie, exactly as better-auth's router does, and core keeps no scheme list (NEST-r2-13).
  - The check runs before resolution, as the router's does, and its verdict is memoized per browser leg, computed from an absolute URL (WebSocket legs used bare paths).
  - Every GraphQL operation a WebSocket carries is enforced, not only subscriptions (ADR-61).
  - Handlers that forward auth cookies get better-auth's form-CSRF rule, public ones included, so login proxies are protected against login CSRF. The rule runs in the guard, so B16 does not count such a handler's `@Public()` as coverage: under `globalGuard: false` it needs `@UseBetterAuth()`.
  - _Rejected in v3:_ keeping an exemption for real HTTP request headers only, and stripping better-auth's cookies from what sources see when it applies (SEC's second option): it changes better-auth's credential precedence and adds a second code path, for clients that already need credentialed CORS and can be added to `trustedOrigins` (§17 Q26); keeping the exemption and checking that the explicit credential authenticated: sources do not report which header authenticated, and better-auth's own rule does not make the distinction either.
- _Evidence:_ LEAD-V16, LEAD-V17, LEAD-V18, LEAD-V33; LEAD-EXP-4; REV-SEC:`probe-bridge-foreign.mjs`; `BA/api/index.ts:285-292`.

**ADR-35. Principal kinds are admitted per route, and delegated principals are never widened. Sources declare `kinds` and `acceptance` (default `'explicit'`); a route accepts the instance's default kinds or `@AcceptPrincipals(...)`, plus the kinds its requirements name; a policy that does not name a kind never receives a principal with `delegation`; built-in policies AND the owner's rights with the credential's own grant (Z5).**

- _Forced by:_ `[R1:BA-r1-01]` and `[R1:SEC-r1-02]` (both blockers). In v1 one source chain served every route, and the admin policy accepted "any kind with a `userId`". A leaked CI key scoped to `{ reports: ['read'] }` and owned by an admin could ban users: `userHasPermission({ userId })` judges the _owner's_ role and never sees the key's permissions. The design's own OAuth example gave a token granted `openid` the user's full rights. Because `PrincipalKinds` is open (R4), every future kind would have inherited the same escalation.
- _Rejected:_
  - BA's minimal fix alone, `requires.principals: ['session']` on the admin policy: authenticated-only routes and every third-party policy that compares `principal.userId` (§4.4.4) would still accept keys and tokens as their owner;
  - accepting every kind everywhere and relying on each policy to check scopes: that is v1, and the PR #94 pitfall in the reference ("never merge role sources implicitly", R:_digest);
  - `acceptance: 'default'` as the default for new sources: registering a source would silently widen every existing route;
  - verifying an unaccepted credential and then answering 403: it spends key quota, writes usage rows and tells an attacker whether a key is valid on routes that never asked for keys. The chain is filtered instead, so the header is treated as absent;
  - an option on `@RequireAuth` (`@RequireAuth({ principals })`, SEC's suggestion) instead of `@AcceptPrincipals`: acceptance is independent of access (`@OptionalAuth()` routes accept kinds too), and a separate decorator composes class-level acceptance with method-level access;
  - core rules for specific kinds ("API keys never pass user-role policies"): R4. The gate compares strings that extensions supply and tests for the presence of a `delegation` field.
- _Rationale:_ a narrow credential reaches a route only if the route, or a policy that can judge it, names its kind. In better-auth's own model such a credential never yields a session, so its admin and organization endpoints are unreachable with it; this reproduces that on Nest routes. `@RequireApiKeyPermission` admits keys on its own route, so the common case needs no second decorator.
- _Evidence:_ `AK/routes/verify-api-key.ts:116-131` (key permissions are a separate scope, checked with `role().authorize`); LEAD-V24 (`hasPermission` grants everything to `adminUserIds`); cases `Z-delegation-scope`, `Z-delegation-unnamed-denied`, `Z-admin-rejects-api-key`, `T-acceptance`.

**ADR-36. Admin-grade decisions read identity authoritatively. A policy declares `requires.freshIdentity`; the planner raises the route's freshness; the admin `permission()` always reads identity authoritatively (an endpoint-produced session past the cookie cache) and passes the role from that session.**

- _Forced by:_ `[R1:SEC-r1-04]`, `[R1:BA-r1-10]`. v1 read the role fresh (by `userId`) but identity from the cookie cache, and claimed parity with better-auth's admin endpoints. REV-SEC:`probe-stale-admin.mjs` disproved it: after admin A was banned, with 0 session rows left, the guard still authenticated A from `session_data` and `userHasPermission(userId)` returned success, while better-auth's `listUsers` answered 401. For a deleted user the same call threw 400 `user not found`, which v1 turned into a 500 per request for up to `cookieCache.maxAge`.
- _Rejected:_
  - keeping cookie-cache identity and documenting the lag (SEC's option 2): a ban that does not take effect on admin routes for five minutes is not what `@RequirePermission` reads like. v2 kept it available per requirement as `freshness: 'cached'` or `'role'`; v3 removed both (below);
  - passing `headers` to `userHasPermission`, so that better-auth does its own authoritative read: a second read, a second API-key validation with `enableSessionForAPIKeys`, and `body.userId`/`body.role` are then ignored (LEAD-V24);
  - forcing authoritative reads on every route: it discards the cookie cache the user configured in `auth.ts`, for routes that make no admin-grade decision;
  - a core rule "admin routes are authoritative": core cannot name a policy (R4). `freshIdentity` is data any policy can declare, and §15.3's role recipe uses it too.
- _Rationale:_ exact parity with `adminMiddleware` (an authoritative session, then that session user's role), at one storage read, the read the route needs anyway. A banned or signed-out admin gets 401 on the next request.
- _Revised in v3_ `[R2:BA-r2-06, BA-r2-05]`: the parity claim held for identity freshness but not for credentials. With `enableSessionForAPIKeys`, the authoritative read went through the hook pipeline, where the api-key plugin answers `/get-session` with a mocked session of the key's owner, so a narrow CI key passed `@RequirePermission` with the owner's admin role, while every better-auth admin endpoint answers 401 for it (REV2-BA:`exp6-apikey-session-admin.mjs`). The authoritative read now accepts only endpoint-produced sessions (ADR-54). The opt-down modes `freshness: 'role'` and `'cached'` were **removed**: both judged a non-authoritative session, key mocks included, with the owner's role, which no better-auth endpoint does. The admin policy keeps its header-less `userHasPermission` call, so it declares `requires.hostlessCalls`, and a dynamic `baseURL` needs a `fallback` (ADR-60).
  - _Rejected in v3:_ BA's option (b), calling `userHasPermission` with the request headers so that better-auth evaluates the identity itself. It costs a second authoritative read (and a second key validation), and its 401 is ambiguous: `getAuthoritativeSessionFromCtx` swallows storage errors into 401 (LEAD-V36), and telling that from "no session" needs a re-resolution, which returns the mocked session again for a key and would answer a leaked key with a 5xx unless the same endpoint-result observation of ADR-54 existed anyway. With it, the one-read path has parity and a clean error classification. Also rejected: keeping the opt-down modes with a token comparison (reduce the headers to cookie and authorization, compare `session.token` with the presented credential), which re-derives cookie names, signature formats and bearer semantics (§17 Q16, Q21).
- _Evidence:_ LEAD-V24; REV-SEC:`probe-stale-admin.mjs`; `BA/plugins/admin/routes.ts:32-45, 1857-1900`; cases `Z-admin-banned`, `Z-admin-deleted-user`; §17 Q16.

**ADR-37. Three memo scopes with three different keys: the principal per logical request (`call.key`; a connection only with a TTL), policy I/O per logical request keyed by concrete inputs, and decisions per handler invocation (`TransportCall.invocation`). Decisions are never keyed by a connection.**

- _Forced by:_ `[R1:NEST-r1-01]` (blocker), `[R1:SEC-r1-13]`. v1 memoized decisions "per request by requirement object identity". A requirement object is created once, when its decorator is evaluated, and GraphQL root fields share the request key by design (S7). `query { a: projects(orgId: "A") b: projects(orgId: "B") }` therefore evaluated `hasPermission` for org A only, and field `b` reused the allow. Apollo batching behaved the same way, and a WebSocket with a principal TTL reused `join A`'s allow for `join B` for the life of the socket.
- _Rejected:_
  - v1's single per-request state;
  - an optional `cacheKey(params, ctx)` on policies (the reviewer's alternative): every policy author has to list every input in the key, and one forgotten input is the same bypass again. The safe default is to share nothing; sharing is opt-in and explicit through `ctx.memo`, where the key _is_ the input;
  - no decision memo at all: B16 makes `@UseBetterAuth()` mandatory on gateways, so on Nest 12 the guard runs twice per message. Without a memo that doubles policy I/O and debug logs. The same invocation always has the same inputs, so sharing within it is safe;
  - caching rejections and infrastructure failures on a connection: a 2 s database blip became minutes of failures per socket.
- _Rationale:_ the two goals of v1's memo are kept apart. S7 (resolve the principal once) needs a request-wide key. Correct authorization needs a key no wider than one evaluation's inputs. Built-in policies keep repeats cheap by deduping better-auth calls on `(endpoint, organization, permissions)`.
- _Revised in v3_ `[R2:NEST-r2-06, NEST-r2-16]`: the principal stamp is no longer one entry per instance on the carrier. Each invocation carries its own result, and the carrier holds results by memo key with a single-entry rule for readers without their own guard run (ADR-30). The source set in the principal key is a content key.
- _Evidence:_ EXP-B:E8; LEAD-V7 (one `args` array per WS message, shared by its guards); graphql-js builds one `info` object per field execution, which is code-derived and pinned by `T-invocation-decisions` (RK3); cases `T-invocation-decisions`, `Z-per-invocation`.

**ADR-38. The mount coordinator prepares the platform on the later of two events, "adapter known" (`HttpAdapterHost.init$`) and "platforms registered" (the default instance's registry factory). A `null` adapter means the app has no HTTP.**

- _Forced by:_ `[R1:NEST-r1-02]`, `[R1:NEST-r1-03]`. v1 selected and prepared the platform inside the `init$` callback, on two wrong assumptions:
  - _"adapter-less bootstraps never emit `init$`"_. They do, with `httpAdapter === null` (LEAD-V26), so `createMicroservice` and `createApplicationContext` crashed in `supports(null)` or failed B08;
  - _"the platforms are known by then"_. Under `NestFactory` the replay runs inside the coordinator's constructor, before any `forRoot` kernel behind an async dependency exists (LEAD-V27).

  Both passed under `@nestjs/testing`, which emits later or not at all, so CI would have stayed green while production could not boot.

- _Rejected:_
  - looking platforms up through `ModuleRef` inside the callback: they do not exist yet;
  - moving Express phase A to `onModuleInit`: Nest has registered its body parsers by then;
  - asking users to call a `prepare(app)` helper in `main.ts`: it breaks `@nestjs/testing` parity and re-creates the reference's "one more required step" support load;
  - letting `platforms` come from `useFactory`: the registry must not wait on runtime options (ADR-22).
- _Rationale:_ nothing depends on the order in which Nest constructs modules, which is concurrent and differs between the two bootstraps. `prepare()` still runs before `NestFactory.create()` resolves and before `createNestApplication()` returns, which is early enough for Express phase A.
- _Revised in v3_ `[R2:NEST-r2-09]`: under `Test…compile()` + `moduleRef.init()` and `Test…createNestMicroservice()`, `init$` never emits and `httpAdapter` is `undefined`. The coordinator records "no HTTP" at `onModuleInit` when nothing was recorded, and an adapter that arrives later fails the app's next `init()` with `LATE_HTTP_ADAPTER` (ADR-62).
- _Evidence:_ REV-NEST:`exp1-init-emission.cjs`, `exp3b-core-module-order-async.cjs`; LEAD-V26, LEAD-V27; LEAD-EXP-3 (event orders on 11.1.17 and 12.0.1, both bootstraps and both adapter-less bootstraps); cases `H-async-options-factory`, `H-no-adapter`.

**ADR-39. The Fastify auth scope installs a child error handler. It answers the canonical 413 for `FST_ERR_CTP_BODY_TOO_LARGE` and hands everything else to the root instance's error handler, which it looks up at request time.**

- _Forced by:_ `[R1:NEST-r1-04]`. Fastify routes capture the error handler that is current when their plugin loads. With `await instance.register()` in `onModuleInit` that is Fastify's default, because Nest calls `setErrorHandler` later, in `registerRouterHooks`. An infrastructure error on an auth route therefore got Fastify's own 500 body, skipped every `APP_FILTER` (Sentry, custom formatting) and was never logged, since Nest creates Fastify with logging off. The 413 body differed from Express's. That broke H8 and H4.
- _Rejected:_
  - registering without `await`, so that the plugin loads at `ready()`, after Nest's handler exists: it also reaches Nest's filters, but route availability then depends on who calls `ready()` and when, and it reopens the draft C claim that EXP-B:E10 refuted;
  - catching in the route handler and invoking Nest's exception layer ourselves: there is no public API for that outside a Nest execution context;
  - setting the **root** error handler ourselves: it would replace Nest's, or be replaced by it;
  - letting Fastify's native 413 body through: "identical on every platform" (H4) is what makes the conformance kit meaningful for third-party platforms.
- _Rationale:_ the handler is explicit and works whenever the plugin loads. `FastifyAdapter.setErrorHandler` always targets the root instance, even with a global prefix (LEAD-V28), so `root.errorHandler` is Nest's by the time a request fails.
- _Evidence:_ REV-NEST:`exp2-fastify-error.cjs`; LEAD-V28; LEAD-EXP-2 (the `APP_FILTER` sees the error and the canonical 413 keeps its CORS header, on 11.1.17 and 12.0.1, both bootstraps, with a global prefix); cases `H-errors-filter-sees`, `H-limit-canonical-body`.

**ADR-40. Every surface the global guard cannot reach fails boot, on every Nest major, by default: WebSocket gateways (`gatewayCoverage`), hybrid-RPC message handlers (`hybridCoverage`), GraphQL field resolvers that carry their own requirements (`fieldResolverCoverage`), controller routes that declare something (B16) under `globalGuard: false`, and handlers with library metadata that no transport serves. Transports claim their handlers in `validate()`; one core rule decides coverage, at the severity each claim carries (`'warn'`/`'off'` relax a transport's own claims).**

- _Forced by:_ `[R1:NEST-r1-05]`/`[R1:SEC-r1-09]`, `[R1:NEST-r1-06]`/`[R1:SEC-r1-10]`, `[R1:NEST-r1-13]`/`[R1:SEC-r1-12]`. v1 failed closed for one gap (Nest 11 gateways, behind a probe) and only documented the other two. A hybrid app that calls `connectMicroservice()` without `inheritAppConfig` gets a fresh `ApplicationConfig`, so `APP_GUARD` never runs for message handlers and any publisher can invoke `billing.refund`. A `@RequirePermission` on a `@ResolveField` is silently not enforced unless `fieldResolverEnhancers` includes `'guards'`, and the default is `[]`.
- _Rejected:_
  - warn by default (the reviewer's option 2): the failure mode is "every requirement on the surface is silently skipped", the same class the design already treated as a boot error for WebSockets;
  - the version probe, and a probe of `@nestjs/websockets` (ADR-18);
  - applying the guard ourselves, by writing guard metadata onto gateways and handlers at boot: it mutates user classes, and its order relative to the user's own guards would be ours to define;
  - detecting `inheritAppConfig`: `connectMicroservice` is called from `main.ts` after the module graph exists, and no provider can observe its second argument. The user asserts it (`rpcTransport({ inheritAppConfig: true })`), and `advise()` prints what the assertion means (RK22);
  - flagging **every** field resolver when `'guards'` is missing: only those whose effective plan carries requirements, or an own access or acceptance decorator other than `@Public()`, would lose a check. Plain field resolvers are untouched.
- _Rationale:_ a requirement the user wrote is either enforced or the app does not start. Where the explicit decorator duplicates a global guard (Nest 12 gateways, hybrid apps that do inherit), the second run is a memo hit (ADR-37).
- _Revised in v3_ `[R2:NEST-r2-02, NEST-r2-11, NEST-r2-12]`: the checks lived inside registered transports, so a forgotten `socketIoTransport()` on Nest 11, a forgotten `rpcTransport()` in a hybrid app, or `globalGuard: false` left written requirements silently unenforced. Coverage is now **one core rule** over data the transports supply: each transport's `validate()` claims the handlers it serves with a reach (`'global'`, `'explicit'`, `'none'`), a code, a hint and a severity, and core fails boot for uncovered claims and, with `UNGUARDED_AUTH_METADATA`, for methods carrying library metadata that no transport claims. An `'explicit'` claim is covered only by the guard **and** the scope interceptor. The WS units find handlers through `'websockets:message_mapping'` and claim a class when they find none. Which handlers need coverage is defined once, in B16 ("declares something"): handler-level declarations and direct-call forwarding, not instance-wide defaults such as `defaultRequirements`. A `public` plan with the form origin check is not covered by its access, because the guard runs that check `[R2:SEC-r2-08]`.
  - _Rejected in v3:_ keeping per-transport checks and adding a core check only for `globalGuard: false` (two rules, and a forgotten transport still passes); requiring coverage for every controller route under `globalGuard: false` (breaks the documented migration path, where routes that declare nothing in B16's sense, `defaultRequirements` notwithstanding, are the app's choice); inferring handlers from Nest metadata in core (core would name transport metadata keys, R4).
- _Evidence:_ LEAD-V6, LEAD-V29, LEAD-V30, LEAD-V32; `core/nest-application.js:207-213` (12.0.1); `graphql/dist/services/resolvers-explorer.service.js:90-104`; the WS, hybrid-RPC and GraphQL matrix jobs (§14.2); §17 Q19.

**ADR-41. Core names no extension. Kind constraints travel as data (`definePrincipalParam`), the no-transport error is generic, every contract can contribute boot advice (`advise()`), and the session's user-id mapping belongs to the session unit.**

- _Forced by:_ `[R1:NEST-r1-07]`. v1 stated R4 and then broke it four times: `principal.kind !== 'session'` in the guard; a `NO_TRANSPORT` message that named `apolloTransport` and its subpath, which needs a context-type-to-package table in core; a boot check (B21) that inspected the jwt, bearer and api-key plugins' options; and an RPC reminder in B22. Each needs a literal that the design's own architecture test bans, so the test would have failed, or the features would have been dropped quietly during implementation.
- _Rejected:_
  - exempting `'session'` from the literal ban: the ban then proves nothing, and a third-party kind that also carries a better-auth session could never satisfy `@CurrentSession()`-style decorators without a core edit;
  - a separate `BootAdvisor` extension point (the reviewer's alternative): a sixth registration list, for something every unit can carry as one optional member;
  - keeping helpful, specific hints in core messages: the hint moves to the unit that knows it. The generic message prints the context type and the registered ids, with a docs link.
- _Rationale:_ the session unit warns about API keys that become sessions (`enableSessionForAPIKeys`; it is the unit registered in that setup, §8.3.1), the RPC unit about hybrid apps, the organization unit about ignored `:orgId` params and the WS units about per-message quota, and core knows none of them. A third-party unit gets the same voice in the boot log.
- _Revised in v3_ `[R2:NEST-r2-08, NEST-r2-04, NEST-r2-13]`: three more pieces of knowledge moved out of core or out of code into data. The `planFor` subclass seam is gone (`defaultRequirements`, ADR-58); a transport supplies a handler's default access (`defaultAccessFor`) and its handler claims; and the origin check no longer holds a list of explicit authorization schemes (ADR-34).
- _Evidence:_ §3.2 rule 5; §14.7 (the ban now holds for v2's pseudo-code); §4 `BootAdvice`.

**ADR-42. `apiKeyPrincipal()` maps `verifyApiKey` results by an explicit table, probes storage when the result is the ambiguous `INVALID_API_KEY`, takes the owner from a `references` option, and declares its side effects as data.**

- _Forced by:_ `[R1:BA-r1-04]`, `[R1:SEC-r1-05]`, `[R1:BA-r1-05]`, `[R1:SEC-r1-14]`. v1 assumed that `verifyApiKey` throws 401 and 429 errors and that `referenceId` is a user id. Neither holds in 1.7.4 (LEAD-V20):
  - the endpoint never throws. A rate-limited key is `{ valid: false, error: { code: 'RATE_LIMITED', details: { tryAgainIn } } }`, so clients got 401 and treated their keys as revoked;
  - a database outage comes back as `INVALID_API_KEY`, the code a missing key gets, so an outage looked like mass key revocation and monitoring saw 4xx (S6);
  - with `references: 'organization'` the id is an organization's.

  Separately, with `enableSessionForAPIKeys` every better-auth call that carries the key spends its quota again (measured 1 → 2 → 3, REV-BA:`probe-apikey-policy.mjs`), and on WebSockets a key is verified, with a write, per message.

- _Rejected:_
  - `valid: false` → 401 across the board (v1);
  - treating `INVALID_API_KEY` as 5xx: anyone can then raise 5xx alarms with random keys;
  - SEC's unthrottled sentinel read on every `INVALID_API_KEY`: a flood of bad keys doubles storage reads. The probe runs at most once per second per instance, and concurrent callers share its result;
  - validating keys against the adapter ourselves: R1. The probe is one read and one no-op write of a random id, a health check;
  - `userId = referenceId` always: an organization id would be judged as a user. Organization keys get `userId: null` and `organizationId`;
  - hiding the quota multiplier by memoizing across different checks: deduping is by concrete inputs only (ADR-37). The multiplier is documented, tested and announced by the session unit's `W_API_KEY_SESSION_MULTIPLIER`; policies flag `presentsCredentials`. The trigger is the api-key plugin's presence, because its options cannot be read, and `session.apiKeySessions` lets the user state the fact (§8.3.1);
  - a default per-connection TTL for quota-consuming sources on WebSockets (SEC's first option): it would introduce revocation lag by default (ADR-18). `effects` drives a boot warning, `W_QUOTA_PER_MESSAGE`, instead.
- _Rationale:_ S6 for a source whose upstream reports failures as values: 429 with `Retry-After` where the key is throttled, 401 where it is bad, 5xx where storage is down.
- _Residual:_ keys held only in secondary storage stay ambiguous (RK18); better-auth logs every failed verification at ERROR (RK19). Both go upstream as a proposal to rethrow non-`APIError` failures.
- _Revised in v3_ `[R2:SEC-r2-02, BA-r2-05]`: the outage probe also runs a no-op write (`updateMany` on a random id), because `verifyApiKey` writes on every call and a store that reads but cannot write returned `INVALID_API_KEY` for every valid key while v2's read-only probe called it healthy (REV2-SEC:`probe-apikey-readonly-db.mjs`; LEAD-EXP-9). `verifyApiKey` receives the request's `Host` when there is one, so a dynamic `baseURL` resolves (ADR-60).
  - _Rejected in v3:_ proving a key exists by looking up its hash (SEC's second suggestion): it reimplements the plugin's hashing and storage lookup (R1).
- _Evidence:_ LEAD-V20, LEAD-V21; REV-BA:`probe-apikey-policy.mjs`; REV-SEC:`probe-apikey-infra.mjs`; `AK/index.ts:166-170` (the plugin object exposes no configuration); cases `S-apikey-results`, `S-apikey-outage`, `S-apikey-org-key`, `Z-apikey-quota-per-request`.

**ADR-43. Infrastructure errors carry a redacted cause that is built fresh from an allow-list, the raw cause is kept behind a non-enumerable slot and an explicit debug option, and transports whose runtime exposes error messages return a generic internal error (`toInternalException`). Request-time configuration errors are generic as thrown (`BetterAuthConfigurationError.atRequest`), because param decorators and services throw them where no transport maps them.**

- _Forced by:_ `[R1:SEC-r1-08]`, `[R1:SEC-r1-19]`. v1 logged infrastructure errors "with their cause chain". Nest's `ConsoleLogger` prints `util.inspect(err)`, which follows `[cause]` and prints enumerable properties (LEAD-V31); pino serializers and Sentry's linked-errors integration read `error.cause` as well. drizzle-orm's `DrizzleQueryError` puts the query parameters into its message **and** into an enumerable `params` property, and `findSession(token)` makes the session token a parameter. A database timeout would have shipped live session and bearer tokens to log aggregators on every guarded request. On GraphQL, request-time `BetterAuthConfigurationError` messages (handler names, instance names, better-auth error text) reached clients, because drivers copy `err.message` into `errors[i].message` even in production. The first fix (`toInternalException`) left the decorators' "No authentication result for SiteController.method" error untouched: it fires exactly when the guard did not run, so no transport mapping applies (post-revision audit of SEC-r1-19).
- _Rejected:_
  - relying on `toInternalException` alone: see above; the param decorators, `defineInvocationParam` decorators and `BetterAuthService` in a resolver body throw outside the guard;
  - a boot check that every handler with a principal or invocation param decorator is covered by `BetterAuthGuard`, **instead of** a safe error (the auditor's alternative). v3's B16 does report claimed handlers with such params that no guard covers (ADR-40, NEST-r2-02). It still cannot prove coverage for a claim relaxed to `'warn'` or `'off'`, handlers in lazily loaded modules, guards applied through another library's composite guard, or guards replaced in tests, so the error must stay safe as thrown;
  - scrubbing the original error's `message` and `stack` in place: the token survives in `params` (LEAD-EXP-6: `util.inspect` still printed it once, and a JSON serializer once). A new `Error` with `name`, `code`, `errno`, `syscall` and a truncated, scrubbed first line carries nothing we did not choose;
  - dropping the cause: operators lose the only diagnostic (`ETIMEDOUT`, the driver's error name);
  - leaving redaction to the user's logger: `pino.redact` matches paths, not substrings of a message;
  - redacting by pattern ("looks like a token"): the kernel knows the exact credential values of the request, which is both stricter and free of false positives;
  - making internal errors intrinsic on GraphQL so that nothing is exposed: nothing would be logged either;
  - genericizing messages on every transport in core: HTTP, WS and RPC runtimes already answer a generic 500 or "Internal server error". The member is optional, so a transport declares its own need. Making the error objects themselves generic (a fixed `message`, the specifics in own properties) needs no transport knowledge, which is why it complements the member rather than replacing it.
- _Rationale:_ §13.4's promise that tokens are never logged now holds for errors the library did not write, and the case `S-log-redaction` pins it on the real logger and on a JSON serializer.
- _Residual:_ values a driver transformed before failing (hashed, truncated, re-encoded) and secrets that are not request credentials (a database password in a connection error) are not scrubbed. First-line truncation bounds the exposure (RK23).
- _Revised in v3_ `[R2:NEST-r2-02]`: B16 now fails boot for claimed handlers with principal or invocation params that no guard covers, which leaves the error to the paths a coverage check cannot see. It stays safe as thrown. `T-internal-error-generic` reaches it through a guard replaced without a stamp, because `globalGuard: false`, which v2's case used, now fails boot for every such handler.
- _Evidence:_ LEAD-V31; LEAD-EXP-6; LEAD-EXP-7 (Apollo 4.13.0 and Mercurius 16.10.0 send a thrown error's `message` and `extensions`, never its other own properties); drizzle-orm 0.45.2 `errors.js:10-19`; cases `S-log-redaction`, `T-internal-error-generic` (including the `unguarded` fixture, reached through a replaced guard since v3).

**ADR-44. The client-IP header's name is random per plugin instance (Web Crypto) unless the user pins one, and platforms report how they trust proxies (`proxyTrust()`), so the two silent rate-limit misconfigurations become visible.**

- _Forced by:_ `[R1:SEC-r1-18]`, `[R1:SEC-r1-06]`.
  - v1's fixed, documented `x-nsba-client-ip` was trusted first by better-auth. Any code path that forwards raw client headers to better-auth (a custom proxy controller, or better-auth's documented `fromNodeHeaders(req.headers)` idiom) let a client pick its rate-limit bucket and its recorded IP. v1 mitigated this with documentation only (RK13).
  - Behind a load balancer with the platform's trust setting at its default, every client has the proxy's IP. Sign-in is limited to 3 per 10 s for the whole user base, and one attacker can lock everyone out. better-auth's own "shared bucket" warning never fires, because the library always supplies a valid IP. With trust-all, clients choose their IP.
- _Rejected:_
  - signing the header value: better-auth's `getIP` reads a header and cannot verify anything;
  - failing boot when trust is `'none'`: that is the correct setting for an app with no proxy in front, and boot cannot tell. The runtime can: the first production request that carries a forwarding header while trust is `'none'` logs `W_PROXY_UNTRUSTED` once;
  - a `node:crypto` random name: the plugin must stay runtime-agnostic (ADR-20);
  - requiring better-auth's `trustedProxies` too: two places to keep in sync (ADR-15).
- _Rationale:_ the name never leaves the process, so it cannot be guessed or probed. Core also strips every inbound `x-nsba-ip-*` header. Proxy trust stays configured once, in the platform, and B27 plus the boot summary make the setting visible.
- _Revised in v3_ `[R2:BA-r2-04]`: the header interacts with better-auth's own proxy trust. When the user set no `ipAddressHeaders`, ours is the only header better-auth reads, and better-auth applies `advanced.ipAddress.trustedProxies` to it, so a deployment configured the better-auth way (`trustedProxies` and no platform trust) resolved every client to no IP and one shared bucket (REV2-BA:`exp4-trustedproxies-header.mjs`). B18 warns about that combination in production, §6.8 documents it, and `W_PROXY_UNTRUSTED` names the outcome. v2's statement that better-auth's shared-bucket warning never fires was corrected.
- _Evidence:_ `CORE/utils/ip.ts:353-384`; `BA/api/rate-limiter/index.ts:342-359, 442-451`; EXP-A:`exp-e2e.mjs`, EXP-B:E9, EXP-C7 (the path, verified with the fixed name); cases `H-ip-spoof`, `H-proxy-trust`; migration step 8 (§15.1).

**ADR-45. App-level extensions (platforms, transports) are declared once, on the default instance: a compile error on named instances and B25 at runtime. An `ExtensionDefinition` can export injectables, which the `forRoot` module re-exports.**

- _Forced by:_ `[R1:NEST-r1-09]`, `[R1:NEST-r1-12]`. v1 merged every instance's lists and de-duplicated by `id`. Two `socketIoTransport()` entries with different `credentials` mappers silently lost one, two unrelated third-party units with the same id lost one, and both contradicted §4.1.1, which says core prints ids and never compares them. Separately, the design told users to inject `WsConnectionAuth`, but nothing provided it, and `ExtensionDefinition` could not export anything.
- _Rejected:_
  - merging with de-duplication by reference and a boot error on id collisions (the reviewer's option 2): it removes the silent drop, but core would compare ids after all, and "which `forRoot` owns the transport list" stays ambiguous;
  - a separate `BetterAuthModule.forApp({ platforms, transports })` call: a second import for the most common, single-instance app;
  - providing `WsConnectionAuth` from the core module: core would import and name an extension (ADR-41). With `exports`, third-party units can offer helper services the same way.
- _Rationale:_ an app has one HTTP adapter and one transport registry, so one declaration site matches reality. An app with named instances must therefore have a default one (`NO_DEFAULT_INSTANCE`). `WsConnectionAuth` is exported under a `Symbol.for` token (`WS_CONNECTION_AUTH`), so it survives a dual-package load.
- _Evidence:_ §4.1.1; R:nest-di §2.3, §3.3; §17 Q20.

**ADR-46. A production boot without a `baseURL` fails (B23 `UNSAFE_BASE_URL`), unless `baseURL` is a dynamic `{ allowedHosts }` config or the user sets `http.allowRequestDerivedBaseURL`.**

- _Forced by:_ `[R1:SEC-r1-07]`. With no `baseURL`, better-auth derives the base URL, token links and a trusted origin from each request. The Express platform builds the URL from `req.host`, that is, from the client's `Host` header. REV-SEC:`probe-unset-baseurl.mjs` requested a password reset for a victim with `Host: evil.example`, and the mailed link pointed at `https://evil.example`: account takeover. better-auth only logs a warning at init, and v1 had no check.
- _Rejected:_
  - a warning: better-auth already prints one, and the consequence is an account takeover, not a degraded feature;
  - a Host allow-list of our own in `AuthExchange`: that is better-auth's `allowedHosts`, reimplemented (R1);
  - failing in every environment: zero-config local development would break, and the attack needs a deployed, reachable app;
  - substituting a guessed origin such as `http://localhost:<port>`: wrong behind any proxy.
- _Rationale:_ fail fast with a copy-paste hint, which is how the design treats every other unsafe configuration. The escape hatch downgrades the error to `W_REQUEST_DERIVED_BASE_URL` for deployments that sanitize `Host` at the edge and accept the residual risk.
- _Revised in v3_ `[R2:BA-r2-05]`: a dynamic `{ allowedHosts }` config without `fallback` is no longer only a warning when units make host-less server calls: better-auth answers every such call with 500, so B20 fails boot then (ADR-60).
- _Evidence:_ `BA/auth/base.ts:76-100`; `BA/context/create-context.ts:152-154`; REV-SEC:`probe-unset-baseurl.mjs`; the security e2e case (§14.4).

**ADR-47. Two better-auth instances in one app must not share cookie names on overlapping scopes (B24 `COOKIE_NAME_COLLISION`).**

- _Forced by:_ `[R1:SEC-r1-11]`. Named instances (ADR-26) keep better-auth's default prefix unless told otherwise, so both used `__Secure-better-auth.session_token` on `Path=/`. With different databases, the admin instance does not know the customer's token and clears the cookie, which logs the customer out of the main app. With a shared database and secret, the customer's token authenticates on the admin instance. Signing in on one mount overwrites the other's session.
- _Rejected:_
  - prefixing cookies per instance ourselves: it means changing `auth.options` after construction (S1), and better-auth's client and other services rely on the names;
  - comparing `advanced.cookiePrefix` only: `advanced.cookies` can rename individual cookies. The check compares the resolved `$context.authCookies` names with their `domain` and `path`;
  - documentation only: the failure is silent cross-instance logout or acceptance.
- _Evidence:_ LEAD-V19; `BA/cookies/index.ts:95-100` (`advanced.cookies.<name>.name` overrides the prefixed name); `BA/api/routes/session.ts:89-92, 288-291`; the §5.5 example sets distinct prefixes; the security e2e case (§14.4).

**ADR-48. Direct `auth.api.*` calls in application code follow better-auth's server-call semantics: their `Set-Cookie` is not forwarded unless the handler, the instance or the call site opts in, and then only for calls that carry the caller's own credential or none.**

- _Forced by:_ `[R1:BA-r1-02]`, `[R1:SEC-r1-03]`. v1's bridge forwarded every non-router call made under the scope interceptor.
  - An admin handler calling `auth.api.signUpEmail({ body })` swapped the admin's browser session for the new user's, because `autoSignIn` is on by default.
  - A service calling `getSession` with a service-account bearer token could hand that session to the end user (REV-SEC:`probe-bridge-foreign.mjs` captured the service account's `session_token`), or clear the user's own cookie when the foreign token had expired.

  In plain better-auth a server call never touches the browser unless the developer adds a cookie plugin or uses `returnHeaders`, and v1's only opt-out was wrapping each call in `runOutsideScope()`.

- _Rejected:_
  - on by default (v1; BA's option 1): the mandatory plugin would keep changing server-call semantics for reasons unrelated to cookies (ADR-02);
  - on by default with a module switch and a boot warning that lists handlers calling credential endpoints (BA's option 3): such calls sit in services and helper functions, and no metadata scan can find them;
  - a hash "fingerprint" of the inbound credential (SEC's sketch): both values live only in the request's memory and are compared, never stored or logged, so hashing adds cost without protection. The comparison is a triple: the session-token cookie (better-auth's own name and parser), `authorization`, and every declared credential header;
  - an allow-list of endpoint paths (sign-in, sign-out): the endpoint set is open, since plugins add their own;
  - a separate `@NoAuthCookies()` decorator (ADR-24).
- _Rationale:_ forwarding is a deliberate act, as adding `nextCookies()` is in better-auth. It needs `@ForwardAuthCookies()`, `cookies.forwardDirectCalls` (B28 warns, because it applies to every handler) or `service.forwardCookies(fn)`. Account switching is explicit too: `{ anyCredential: true }`. The library's own policy calls always forward, because they carry the request's credential by construction. The docs also state that direct credential calls bypass better-auth's rate limiter and origin check, which are router-only.
- _Evidence:_ `BA/api/routes/sign-up.ts:431-441`; `BA/integrations/next-js.ts:95-139`; REV-SEC:`probe-bridge-foreign.mjs`; cases `S-bridge-third-party-signup`, `S-bridge-foreign-credentials`; §17 Q13, RK14.

**ADR-49. Hook fidelity: the database dispatcher mirrors better-auth per operation, database-hook types are derived from `BetterAuthOptions['databaseHooks']`, a throwing matcher propagates as it does in better-auth, and hook bodies are typed as unvalidated input.**

- _Forced by:_ `[R1:BA-r1-06]`, `[R1:BA-r1-07]`, `[R1:BA-r1-08]`. Four places where v1 promised more, or something other, than better-auth delivers:
  - it chained merged data through `update.before` hooks, where better-auth passes every hook the **original** payload and chains only on create;
  - it typed `update` payloads as the full model (they are `Partial`) and allowed `{ data }` from `delete.before` (better-auth ignores it);
  - it swallowed a throwing predicate, so the hook silently did not run, where better-auth answers 500 for before-hook matchers and propagates after-hook ones;
  - it typed `ctx.body` with the endpoint's validated schema, although hooks run before validation: `ctx.body.email.toLowerCase()` type-checked and then threw on `{ "email": 123 }`, turning a 400 into a 500.
- _Rejected:_
  - hand-written payload types: they drift. Types evaluated in the user's program follow the better-auth version that is installed there;
  - `DeepPartial<BodyAt<P>>` for bodies (the reviewer's first suggestion): it still claims value types, and plain `unknown` loses key autocomplete. `UnvalidatedBody<B>` keeps the keys and types every value `unknown`;
  - validating the body ourselves before the before-hooks: it reimplements better-call's validation (R1) and would run it twice.
- _Rationale:_ a Nest hook must be indistinguishable from the same function written as a native plugin. `LIB-dispatcher-parity` now covers update, updateMany, delete and throwing matchers.
- _Revised in v3_ `[R2:BA-r2-02, BA-r2-07]`: the update dispatcher returned the original payload merged with the hooks' data, and better-auth merges that over what earlier plugins changed, which reverted them; it now returns only what the hooks returned (LEAD-EXP-10), and `LIB-dispatcher-parity` puts a modifying plugin in front of both setups. The replacement advice of v2 for rules on the resolved session, `@AfterAuth('/get-session')`, is scoped to Nest routes: better-auth's own endpoints read the session with a plain call that skips hooks (§10.4).
- _Evidence:_ LEAD-V22, LEAD-V23; better-call `context.ts:203-219`; `CORE/types/init-options.ts:1405-1470`; §14.5, including the test `LIB-hook-bearer-client`.

**ADR-50. With `onAPIError: { throw: true }`, `AuthExchange` rethrows an `APIError` unchanged to the host error pipeline. Without it, a thrown `APIError` becomes its Response.**

- _Forced by:_ `[R1:BA-r1-09]`. Teams set that option so auth-route errors reach their Nest filters. better-auth's router then rethrows out of `auth.handler` (LEAD-V25). v1 caught the error with `isAPIError` and rebuilt a JSON Response, so the option silently did nothing. The conversion was also a hand-written copy of better-call's `toResponse`.
- _Rejected:_
  - always converting (v1);
  - always rethrowing: `auth.handler` also throws `APIError`s that are not the user's choice (an init failure, a disallowed dynamic host). Those would surface as Nest's default 500 and lose better-auth's status and its cleanup cookies.
- _Rationale:_ the user's better-auth configuration decides, as it does everywhere else. The error keeps its hidden `better-call:api-error-headers`, so a filter can restore cookies. On Fastify the rethrow goes through the child error handler to Nest's (ADR-39).
- _Evidence:_ LEAD-V25; `BA/auth/base.ts:107-108`; H13; case `H-errors-apierror-throw`.

**ADR-51. Consumer test helpers cover both guard registrations and cooperate with exclusive binding: `overrideAuthGuard` overrides the provider **and** the guard (and the interceptor) and can stamp a principal; `stampPrincipal()` is public; `initTestApp` closes the previous test app bound to the same instance.**

- _Forced by:_ `[R1:NEST-r1-08]`, `[R1:SEC-r1-15]`.
  - `overrideProvider` replaces only what `APP_GUARD` aliases, and `overrideGuard` replaces only the injectables that `@UseGuards` creates per host module. B16 makes `@UseBetterAuth()` mandatory on gateways, so v1's helper left the real guard running exactly there. Where the override did apply, `@CurrentSession()` threw, because a stand-in guard had no way to publish a resolution.
  - v1's `initTestApp` closed apps in `afterAll`, so an app built per test hit `INSTANCE_ALREADY_BOUND` on the second test.
- _Rejected:_
  - documenting "call both override methods": that is the trap the helper exists to remove;
  - making the param decorators tolerate a missing resolution: it would bring back the reference's silent `undefined` (#12; ADR-30);
  - registering close with `afterEach` when one is in scope: the helper is runner-agnostic, and it would not cover a failed `init()` (ADR-25). An explicit `closeWith` option covers runners.
- _Rationale:_ `overridePrincipal` stays the recommended tool, because it keeps the real guard, acceptance, origin check and policies. The guard override exists for tests that want none of them.
- _Refined after the post-revision audit:_ a stand-in guard publishes through a test stamp verified by args-element identity (§7.8 item 3), and both scope interceptors copy it into the scope. The carrier stamp alone did not work on WebSocket gateways, which have no carrier, and the stand-in interceptor now explicitly opens the scope.
  - _Rejected:_ stamping the socket (races across concurrent messages); stamping only the args array (on HTTP the router passes guards and interceptors different arrays, LEAD-V34); having `stampPrincipal()` look up the transport (a free function in a test has no DI access).
- _Revised in v3_ `[R2:NEST-r2-15]`: `overridePrincipal` could not exercise organization requirements (their endpoints need a real session), and no seam could stub a decision, because policies travel by reference in metadata. The evaluator calls policies through `POLICY_INVOKER`, and `overrideDecisions(builder, decide)` wraps it; `undefined` runs the real policy. `overridePrincipal`'s resolver answers the evaluator's re-classification read (`bypassMemo`, §8.1) `absent`, so an organization requirement without a stub denies 401 instead of failing as infrastructure (§14.8).
- _Evidence:_ `core/injector/module.js:344-356`; LEAD-V7; LEAD-V34; §14.8, tests `LIB-testing-override-principal` and `LIB-testing-stamp-mock-guard`.

**ADR-52. Diagnostics never change a response. Unknown paths under the mount stay better-auth's bodiless 404s, and outside production each one is logged once with a "did you mean", capped at 100 distinct paths.**

- _Forced by:_ `[R1:SEC-r1-16]`. A client `baseURL` of `/api/auth/api/auth`, or a call to `/api/auth/signin/email`, reaches better-auth, which answers 404 with no body, and nothing is logged. Misconfiguration was about 20% of the reference's issues, and this was its largest cluster (R:_digest, ref-issues cluster 1).
- _Rejected:_
  - adding a body or a header to the 404: auth-route responses are verbatim (H7), and clients may depend on better-auth's exact shape;
  - on in production by default: scanners would turn every probed path into a WARN line. It is off there unless `http.diagnostics: true`, and capped either way;
  - failing boot on "suspicious" base paths: no static signal separates a wrong client URL from a right one.
- _Rationale:_ the log line names the resolved base path and the closest of `auth.api[*].path`, the list B12 already builds, which is what a developer needs to see the doubled prefix or the typo. `W_PROXY_UNTRUSTED` (ADR-44) follows the same rule: say it once, never touch the response.
- _Evidence:_ R:ref-issues cluster 1; §6.3 step 7; case `H-diagnostics-404`.

**ADR-53. Hooks bind in the core module's `onModuleInit`. better-auth calls made before that are counted by the plugin and reported at boot (B26); they are not prevented.**

- _Forced by:_ `[R1:NEST-r1-11]`. v1 claimed that the global core module always initializes first. Nest gives every global module the same distance and keeps insertion order among them (LEAD-V27), so a `@Global() DatabaseModule` imported before `BetterAuthModule` whose `onModuleInit` seeds users through `auth.api.signUpEmail` runs **before** hooks are bound. The plugin is inert until binding, so `@BeforeDatabase('user.create')` normalization and audit hooks were silently skipped for the seeded users.
- _Rejected:_
  - binding earlier, in a constructor: hook providers from other modules may not exist yet, and discovery needs the whole graph;
  - throwing on a dispatch before binding: the plugin must stay inert when unbound, because the same `auth.ts` serves scripts, the better-auth CLI and non-Nest code (§10.2);
  - queueing early calls until binding: a seeding call awaits its result, so that deadlocks.
- _Rationale:_ the claim is narrowed to what Nest guarantees (the core module runs before non-global modules' hooks). The plugin's first before-hook matcher counts dispatches while unbound, at no cost on the bound path, and `W_CALLS_BEFORE_BIND` tells the user how many calls ran without hooks and to move seeding to `onApplicationBootstrap`.
- _Revised in v3_ `[R2:NEST-r2-10]`: the counter also counts database-hook dispatches while unbound, so seeding through `internalAdapter` in another global module's `onModuleInit`, which never dispatches an endpoint, is reported too.
- _Evidence:_ LEAD-V27; `core/injector/container.js:104-109`; §5.4, §10.3.

**ADR-54. An authoritative identity read accepts only a session the get-session endpoint itself produced. The `nestjs()` plugin observes that through an after-hook, because a before-hook short-circuit skips every after-hook; a short-circuited dispatch's missing `Headers` is tolerated.**

- _Forced by:_ `[R2:BA-r2-06]` (blocker), `[R2:BA-r2-01]`. With `apiKey({ enableSessionForAPIKeys: true })` the api-key plugin answers `/get-session` with a mocked session of the key's owner (LEAD-V38). v2's authoritative read went through the hook pipeline, so a CI key granting `{ project: ['read'] }` passed `@RequirePermission({ user: ['ban'] })` with its owner's admin role, while better-auth's `listUsers`, `banUser` and `userHasPermission` answer 401 for the same key, because `getAuthoritativeSessionFromCtx` discards hook-provided sessions and re-reads without hooks (LEAD-V36; REV2-BA:`exp6-apikey-session-admin.mjs`). The escalation was reachable as written on WebSockets, RPC and subscriptions; on HTTP a second bug hid it: the short-circuit returns `headers: undefined`, which the session source dereferenced, so every key request answered 500 (REV2-BA:`exp1-apikey-returnheaders.mjs`).
- _Decision:_ the session source reads `result.headers?.getSetCookie() ?? []`, and on an authoritative plan it returns `absent` unless `AuthHandle.producedByEndpoint(result.response)`. The plugin's after-hook entry 4 records the final `ctx.context.returned` object of every non-router dispatch in a `WeakSet` while bound (§10.2). Default-freshness routes still accept key sessions, as better-auth's `sessionMiddleware` endpoints do.
- _Rejected:_
  - comparing the session's token with the presented cookie or bearer credential after reducing the headers (BA's first suggestion): it re-derives cookie names, signature formats, bearer semantics and multi-session behavior, and a plugin may read keys from `authorization` itself;
  - detecting the short-circuit from `headers === undefined`: a hook that set a response header before short-circuiting produces `Headers` (LEAD-V37);
  - calling better-auth's admin evaluation with the request headers instead (BA's option (b), ADR-36): a second read, and a 401 that cannot be classified without this very observation;
  - rejecting key sessions everywhere: better-auth accepts them on ordinary and organization endpoints, so that would be a divergence of its own.
- _Rationale:_ the rule is better-auth's (an authoritative session is what the plain `getSession` produces from the request's headers), and the observation uses only the documented hook contract. LEAD-EXP-8 shows the recorded set agrees with better-auth's admin verdict for cookie, bearer, key-session, short-circuit and replaced-result requests, with and without `customSession`, on 1.7.0 and 1.7.4. The one disagreement, a request carrying both a cookie and a key, is answered more strictly (401) and documented (RK27).
- _Evidence:_ LEAD-V36, LEAD-V37, LEAD-V38; LEAD-EXP-8; REV2-BA:`exp1-apikey-returnheaders.mjs`, `exp6-apikey-session-admin.mjs`; cases `S-short-circuit-session`, `Z-admin-rejects-api-key-session`, `LIB-authoritative-session`.

**ADR-55. Route plans are compiled and cached per (controller class, handler), and the guard reads the plan before it selects a transport: `inherit` plans, and `public` plans without the form origin check, return without one.**

- _Forced by:_ `[R2:NEST-r2-01]` (blocker), `[R2:NEST-r2-03]`. Nest gives every subclass the same handler function for an inherited route method (REV2-NEST:`exp1-inherited-handler.mjs`), so v2's per-handler cache let the first request of a generic `CrudController` subclass decide the plan of every other subclass: a `@Public()` subclass requested first made its `@RequirePermission` sibling public. Separately, v2 selected the transport before reading `@Public()`, and `rpcTransport().handles()` required a carrier match, so credential-less TCP messages and public handlers in context types no transport serves (a `@golevelup/nestjs-rabbitmq` `'rmq'` handler, which global guards reach, REV2-NEST:`exp3-external-context-global-guard.mjs`) answered 500 `NO_TRANSPORT`.
- _Decision:_ `WeakMap<Type, WeakMap<Function, RoutePlan>>`; the boot scan compiles the same pairs. The guard's order is plan; exit for `inherit` plans and for `public` plans whose origin check is not `'form'`; transport; origin check; exit for the remaining `public` plans (a `@ForwardAuthCookies()` login proxy, after its form check, SEC-r2-08); resolution; acceptance; evaluation (§7.1). `handles()` must not depend on credentials (T1); the RPC transport handles every `'rpc'` context and chooses the carrier in `describe()`.
- _Rejected:_ caching by handler and documenting "do not share route methods through inheritance" (a common Nest pattern, and the failure is an authorization bypass); keying by `ctx.getClass().name` (two classes can share a name across modules); selecting a transport for public handlers to stamp an `absent` result (B15 already forbids principal params there, and the stamp was the only reason).
- _Evidence:_ REV2-NEST:`exp1-inherited-handler.mjs`, `exp3-external-context-global-guard.mjs`; cases `T-inherited-handler`, `T-public-unclaimed-context`, `T-no-credentials`, planner unit tests.

**ADR-56. A transport may supply a handler's default access. The GraphQL transports answer `'inherit'` for field resolvers without their own or class-level access, acceptance or requirement metadata: the guard returns at once, and decorators read the root field's result.**

- _Forced by:_ `[R2:NEST-r2-04]`, `[R2:SEC-r2-09]`. Once an app followed B16's own hint (`fieldResolverEnhancers: ['guards']`), every undecorated field resolver got `defaultAccess: 'authenticated'`, so anonymous public queries failed at the first field resolver, once per list item (REV2-NEST:`exp2-field-resolver-default-access.mjs`). Without the enhancer the same field resolvers ran unguarded while the developer believed `defaultAccess` applied, and nothing warned.
- _Decision:_ `AuthTransport.defaultAccessFor(target, method)` sits between class-level metadata and `defaultAccess` in the planner (§7.6). An `inherit` plan does no I/O and needs no coverage. The GraphQL units warn (`W_FIELD_RESOLVER_INHERITS`) when public or optional root fields and inheriting field resolvers coexist, and B22 counts inheriting handlers.
- _Rejected:_ `defaultAccess` for field resolvers (NEST's option B: fixing one guarded field resolver breaks every public query app-wide); a planner rule that names GraphQL metadata (core would read an extension's metadata key, R4); computing reachability from root fields through the schema to warn precisely (needs the built schema at boot and type-level analysis for a warning).
- _Rationale:_ a field resolver is reached only through a root field the guard already decided, so inheriting that decision is the GraphQL meaning of the request, and the declarative escape (`@RequireAuth()` on the field) stays available.
- _Evidence:_ REV2-NEST:`exp2-field-resolver-default-access.mjs`; LEAD-V30; cases `T-inherit-no-lookup`, the GraphQL job (§14.2); §17 Q23.

**ADR-57. The principal is read, never resolved, outside the guard: `BetterAuthService.principalFor(ctx)` serves guards and interceptors; `getPrincipal()`/`getSession()` return the guard's result in a handler scope, `null` on public plans, and throw `NO_AUTH_SCOPE` outside a handler scope.**

- _Forced by:_ `[R2:NEST-r2-07]`, `[R2:SEC-r2-04]`. No API read the principal from an `ExecutionContext`, and `getPrincipal()` returned `null` outside the scope, the value that also means anonymous, so migrated custom guards (`SubscriptionActiveGuard`, a user-keyed throttler) silently treated every user as anonymous. Separately, `getPrincipal()` resolved lazily inside a public handler's scope, after the guard had returned before the origin check, so a cross-site form post to a public unsafe route acted as the victim.
- _Decision:_ §7.8. `principalFor` peeks the resolver under the plan's memo key, then the stamps; services never start a resolution.
- _Rejected:_
  - returning `undefined` outside a scope and `null` for anonymous (NEST's option C): callers must check `=== null`, and the silent path remains;
  - SEC's recommended option, lazy resolution on public routes with the origin check applied at that point: a second path into the resolver with its own origin handling, to save one cookie-cache hit per request on routes that want an optional identity, which `@OptionalAuth()` already provides after the check (§17 Q27);
  - a free function `getAuthResult(ctx)`: stamps alone cannot reach the resolver's settled entry, and every guard that needs it can inject the service.
- _Evidence:_ `reviews/round-2-SEC.md` (the SEC-r2-04 scenario); cases `LIB-principal-for`, `T-public-service-null`; §17 Q24, Q27.

**ADR-58. Company-wide requirements are a runtime option, `defaultRequirements`, compiled into every `required` plan. `BetterAuthGuard` has no subclass seam.**

- _Forced by:_ `[R2:NEST-r2-08]`. v2 documented a protected `planFor` override for "a company-wide default requirement", but the subclass could not be registered where it mattered: `globalGuard` aliases `BetterAuthGuard`, `@UseBetterAuth()` applies `BetterAuthGuard`, and coverage recognized only `BetterAuthGuard`. Gateways and hybrid handlers therefore ran the base guard without the requirement (fail-open), and boot validation, the scope interceptor and the decorators all read planner plans that lacked it; v2 needed a runtime param-kind safety net only for those plans.
- _Decision:_ §7.6 step 4. The runtime comparison of principal kinds with param decorators is removed with the seam (ADR-29).
- _Rejected:_ wiring a guard subclass through `globalGuard`, `@UseBetterAuth()`, coverage and the scan (NEST's option B: class identity across call sites and dual packages, for something plans express as data); a `PlanContributor` extension point (a sixth registration list for what a requirement list already expresses; it can be added later without breaking the option).
- _Evidence:_ design-v2 §2.2.2, §5.7, §7.6 step 6; cases `T-reads-session` (third boot), planner unit tests; §17 Q25.

**ADR-59. An `APIError` 401 that escapes a policy is re-classified by one authoritative re-resolution of the principal, outside the memo: still authenticated → 5xx; no longer → 401 `UNAUTHENTICATED`.**

- _Forced by:_ `[R2:BA-r2-03]`. better-auth's `getSessionFromCtx` catches every error into `null`, so its `sessionMiddleware` answers 401 `UNAUTHORIZED` for a storage failure (LEAD-V36). An organization check during a brownout, after the guard's read succeeded, returned 401, and v2's safety net ("401 or 403 becomes deny 403") answered 403 "no permission", logged at debug (REV2-BA:`exp3-org-outage-401.mjs`). A session revoked between the two reads also became 403 instead of 401.
- _Decision:_ Z2 and §8.1. Built-in organization policies map only the membership codes and let other `APIError`s escape. The re-resolution goes through the resolver with the plan's accepted kinds and `freshness: 'authoritative'` (so a hook-provided session is not accepted, ADR-54), at most once per invocation.
- _Rejected:_ always 401 (BA's option (b): outages look like logouts); always 5xx (option (c): a revoked session answers 500); a storage health probe like the API-key one (it cannot tell "this session is gone" from "storage is fine", and the secondary-storage case differs); calling a session-free variant of the organization endpoints (none exists).
- _Rationale:_ the same trade ADR-42 makes for `INVALID_API_KEY`: one extra read on a rare path keeps S6 true.
- _Evidence:_ LEAD-V36; REV2-BA:`exp3-org-outage-401.mjs`; cases `Z-policy-session-lost`, `Z-infra-throws`, `Z-apierror-mapping`; §17 Q22.

**ADR-60. Units declare host-less server calls (`requires.hostlessCalls` on policies, principal sources and transports). A dynamic `baseURL` without `fallback` fails boot when any registered or referenced unit declares them.**

- _Forced by:_ `[R2:BA-r2-05]`. For a dynamic `baseURL`, better-auth resolves a direct call's base URL from its `Host` header and throws 500 without one and without `fallback` (REV2-BA:`exp5-dynamic-baseurl-headerless.mjs`). The admin policy calls `userHasPermission` without headers by design, `apiKeyPrincipal()` called `verifyApiKey` without headers, and RPC carriers copy no `Host`: each failed every request while HTTP, GraphQL and WebSocket traffic kept working, so the app booted and smoke tests passed.
- _Decision:_ B20 is an error in that combination and names the units; the admin policy and `rpcTransport()` declare host-less calls; `apiKeyPrincipal()` passes the request's `Host` and declares nothing.
- _Rejected:_ passing a `Host` on the admin call (with any headers, `userHasPermission` demands a session and answers 401); substituting `fallback` ourselves (a guessed origin, ADR-46); warning only (the failure is total for those routes).
- _Evidence:_ REV2-BA:`exp5-dynamic-baseurl-headerless.mjs`; `BA/api/to-auth-endpoints.ts:36-67`; `BA/context/helpers.ts:175-189`; cases `Z-admin-dynamic-base-url`, `S-dynamic-base-url`, the base-URL matrix axis.

**ADR-61. GraphQL transports classify an operation by its carrier before its kind: every operation a WebSocket carries gets the subscription treatment (cookie-less, per-operation key, the upgrade request as an enforced browser leg).**

- _Forced by:_ `[R2:SEC-r2-03]`. graphql-ws executes queries and mutations sent over the socket, and Nest passes `execute` to it; Mercurius does the same with `fullWsTransport`. v2 classified by operation kind, so a query over a hijacked socket was treated as an HTTP query: no origin check, and a principal memoized on the connection-lifetime upgrade request.
- _Decision:_ §9.2. Recognition covers Nest's default Apollo context, custom contexts exposing the upgrade request, and Mercurius; the path is UNVERIFIED until the conformance cases for every operation kind and context shape pass (RK3).
- _Rejected:_ rejecting non-subscription operations over WebSockets (legitimate clients use graphql-ws for everything); enforcing only mutations over the socket (a hijacked socket reads query replies).
- _Evidence:_ graphql-ws 6.0.7 `dist/server-3ewaJSjp.js:209-214` and 6.2.1 `dist/server-DHPI7HHW.js:210-215` (pinned by @nestjs/graphql 13.2.4 and 14.0.0); @nestjs/graphql 13.2.4 `gql-subscription.service.js:31-36`, 14.0.0 `:17-26`; @nestjs/apollo 13.2.4 `apollo-base.driver.js:196-228`; mercurius 16.10.0 `subscription-connection.js:247-266`; cases `T-subscription-origin`, `T-memo-once`.

**ADR-62. The core module's lifecycle work runs once per application, and "no adapter yet" at `onModuleInit` means no HTTP.**

- _Forced by:_ `[R2:NEST-r2-05]`, `[R2:NEST-r2-09]`. `NestMicroservice.init()` runs `onModuleInit` and `onApplicationBootstrap` twice; v2's second binding attempt found its own bootstrapped binding and threw `INSTANCE_ALREADY_BOUND`, so `createMicroservice(...)` + `init()` could not start (REV2-NEST:`exp4b-double-init.mjs`, `exp4c-microservice-init-twice.mjs`, both majors). Under `Test…compile()` + `moduleRef.init()` and `createNestMicroservice()`, `init$` never emits and `httpAdapter` is `undefined`, a state v2 left unspecified.
- _Decision:_ `InstanceRegistry` holds the lifecycle state; repeated calls return; `bind()` from the same owner is a no-op; the coordinator records `httpAdapter ?? null` at `onModuleInit` and reports a later adapter with `LATE_HTTP_ADAPTER` (§5.7).
- _Rejected:_ detecting `NestMicroservice` (a class check on another package, and a future Nest could call hooks twice elsewhere); unbinding and rebinding on the second call (a window without hooks during boot).
- _Evidence:_ REV2-NEST:`exp4-testing-no-init.mjs`, `exp4b-double-init.mjs`, `exp4c-microservice-init-twice.mjs`; `@nestjs/microservices` 11.1.17 `nest-microservice.js:69-81, 162-169`; cases `H-no-adapter`, `H-late-adapter`, lifecycle unit tests.

**ADR-63. Organization refs resolve to an organization ID that the policies validate and always send: the default ref reads the session's active organization ID (or asks `getActiveMember` for a custom session shape without it); anything but a non-empty string is "no organization". No slug ref ships.**
